item.title: The Architect, the Paranoid, the Dreamer, and Other Employees of the Future IT Company
item.description:
In recent years, writing working code has become almost trivially easy, while building a good software system has become harder. Today, someone without a traditional IT background can, in an evening, assemble an interface, API, database, and even deploy something. And then the real fun begins: the architecture starts to fall apart, dependencies take on a life of their own, security appears in "version 2.0," and no one really understands why the system works at all. I wrote this article after observing colleagues, students, and acquaintances who are increasingly using AI for development. And I caught myself thinking: AI has made code production cheaper, but it has hardly made understanding what code to produce any cheaper. Hence the main question: what should a small IT company look like if a significant part of the work can already be done by digital performers? I present my controversial model of such a company: a smart analyst, an architect-developer, a super-tester, a dreamer, a DevOps engineer, and a security paranoid. Plus, the company's collective memory, because without it, neural networks quickly start reinventing the architecture from scratch. Perhaps half of these roles could indeed be filled by one person in slippers. But then, an unpleasantly large number of requirements arise for that person... What have you invented now?

item.title: Preparing a Dataset for Offline Evaluation of Recommender Models: What to Check Before Running Experiments
item.description:
Hello, Habr! My name is Alexey Vasiliev, and I am the team lead of the "Recommender Systems and Personalization" team at Sber AI Lab, Sber's Center for Practical Artificial Intelligence. We conduct research in the field of recommendations, develop new models, and, of course, compare our results with those of colleagues and other researchers. We regularly encounter situations where results claimed in a scientific paper or obtained from another team cannot be reproduced, even though the key parameters of the pipeline are identical. In this article, my colleague Anna Volodkevich and I will share our experience analyzing such discrepancies, which led us to develop the SplitLight framework. When the results of a scientific paper or the success of another team cannot be reproduced, people usually start by looking for bugs in the model implementation: they examine the architecture, loss function, and negative sampling method. While some discrepancies are indeed due to these factors, our practical experience shows that the data preparation procedure often has a greater impact on the final result of comparing recommender models. For example, the statement from a paper "Zvuk dataset, global temporal split with a quantile of 0.9" does not specify which filters and aggregations were applied, how events with identical timestamps and repeated interactions were handled, whether cold objects were removed, what data was fed to the model, and based on which events metrics were calculated. Therefore, two pipelines with the same dataset and the same split name might be evaluating different problem formulations. This hinders experiment reproducibility and comparison of results across works. Read more

item.title: What the Default Assistant on Android Can Do - Using Alice AI as an Example
item.description:
On Android devices, you can choose a default assistant, much like a browser. Once selected in settings, you can invoke it with a system gesture over any app. Convenient. You might think that the chosen assistant can now see everything on your phone and do whatever it wants... Not at all. When installed, Android grants an app only basic permissions. Access to advanced features requires separate user permission, and some functions are entirely unavailable to regular third-party apps. My name is Vanya, I lead the Android development team for Alice's SDK and am the tech lead for the default assistant project. Today, we'll explore these boundaries using Alice AI as an example. Read more

Hello! My name is Vladislav Kozlov, and I am the lead of Business Security analysts at Avito. I want to share an interesting experience with LLM that allowed me to cheaply and quickly test my idea. I'll also tell you about an interesting clustering algorithm that my model and I came up with and implemented as a library. item.title: CMF: A New Format for Creating Specialized LLM Models
item.description:
CMF is a new format for neural networks. This article explains how CMF differs from GGUF and SafeTensors, and how multiple capabilities can be layered onto a common structure without storing separate full models. This is the first detailed open publication of the CMF format, and it can already be used in your own projects. item.title: [Translation] 14 Reasons Why Robotics Is Hard
item.description:
AI development is moving forward, but almost all visible progress is in the realm of knowledge work, i.e., actions that occur inside a computer. Among AI developers in San Francisco, there is a widespread opinion that robots will soon join this sphere. Parallel to the race for general-purpose AI development is an equally aggressive race for general-purpose robots – humanoid machines with physical intelligence. Artificial workers capable of cooking and cleaning, being loaders... and doing everything else, including producing their own kind, leading (according to many forecasts) to economic growth characterized as 'explosive'. In other words, the prevailing opinion is that AI in data centers will soon replace all intellectual labor, and AI in humanoid bodies will soon replace all physical labor. However, there is an important difference: we are already seeing progress in intellectual labor, but physical AI largely remains confined to test sites and demonstration videos. There is no robot equivalent to ChatGPT that we can buy. Therefore, we have to limit ourselves to video demonstrations. Unfortunately, this tool is not well-suited for assessing progress. We may be seeing one successful attempt out of a hundred failures. The demonstration scenario can be carefully crafted to avoid complexities that the robot is not yet ready for. The video can be edited to make it seem like the robot acts faster and more clearly than it actually does. There is an example of a very impressive demonstration... with a suspiciously large number of camera angle changes. (I haven't seen almost any videos from the recent World Humanoid Robot Games yet. They are valuable because there are fewer opportunities for selective presentation of facts on a public platform. In a couple of videos I watched, impressive capabilities can be seen, but they don't touch upon many of the complexities I've listed below... Also, these videos have many high-profile failures.) Demonstrations draw attention to what robots can already do. The question arises: what can't they do? In this post, I will list the technical challenges we need to overcome to realize general-purpose artificial workers. The next time you see a robot doing something impressive, ask yourself: which of the capabilities listed in the article did the robot demonstrate, and which complexities did the video scenario try to bypass? (It's worth noting that some tasks become easier if wheeled robots are used instead of strictly humanoid ones. A wheeled robot can carry more weight, so power, endurance, and electronics power are less critical for it. The probability of falling is also lower for it. However, such robots cannot climb stairs, step over obstacles, or bend down to pick something from a cabinet.) Read more

item.title: How AI is Changing Pharma: AstraZeneca's Experience in Russia and the World
item.description:
Pharma is an industry with long cycles, complex processes, and a high cost of error. This is especially evident in the drug development path: from identifying a promising molecule and preclinical studies to multiple phases of clinical trials, registration, and market launch. On average, developing one drug takes 10-15 years and costs around $1-2 billion, and of the candidates that reach clinical studies, nine out of ten do not reach registration. We won't write an article in the style of 'we implemented AI -> things got better.' There are already many such materials on Habr, and due to the prevalence and widespread cult of AI, they may not inspire trust. We are more interested in showing what is changing in the very logic of how pharma works, using specific examples. Read more

item.title: Component Tokens in 15 Minutes Instead of Two Days Using AI: Step-by-Step Process and Pitfalls
item.description:
The first component took us two days to assemble, the fifteenth took fifteen minutes. All that appeared between them is the DESIGN.md file, a set of rules, and an understanding of where the neural network invents aliases that never existed in the system. Hello, Habr! My name is Ekaterina, I am a product designer and I am developing the Sova design system within the "Lukomorye" ecosystem. We needed to connect design, tokens, and code at the component level. To do this, we had to describe each component in detail: sizes, variants, states, paddings, colors. Doing this manually can take a long time, so we handed over the mechanical part to the neural network. It didn't work out the first time. Below is the entire process: how we exported components from Pixso, what we wrote in markdown files with rules and templates, and how we then checked that the neural network hadn't made anything up. Read more

item.title: Digital Amnesia: Why a Total Human Exclusion AI Strategy in Banks Might Lead to a Dead End?
item.description:
My recent interactions with Russian banks prompted me to investigate how decisions are currently made regarding ordinary depositors. It's clear that all banks use AI systems to varying degrees, with each having a unique decision-making algorithm shaped by their individual AI policies. This article reviews existing AI systems in the banking sector with real-world examples. 1. What differentiates banking AI systems? International classification: HITL, HOTL, and HOOTL. 1) Human-in-the-Loop (HITL): Humans are directly involved in every system cycle. AI performs tasks or suggests options, but the final decision or approval of each step remains with the human. Example: HSBC, BNP Paribas. Europe is under immense pressure from the EU AI Act. Article 14 mandates that financial institutions develop high-risk AI systems that can be "effectively controlled by natural persons." Case: Consumer loans and mortgages. How it works: AI calculates a credit score using hundreds of parameters, but if the model's confidence level is below 95%, the system must forward the application to a human loan officer. HSBC has established a special AI Review Committee to personally validate algorithm logic in disputed cases. HSBC surveys show that 62% of wealthy European investors demand a human advisor, not an algorithm, for final decisions. Read more

item.title: Tensor Cores Are No Longer Enough: Why AI Accelerators Will Hit a Memory Wall
item.description:
AI accelerator manufacturers continue to increase the number of tensor cores and adopt shorter data formats like FP8 and FP4. Performance seems to be growing at an impressive rate, but there's a catch. Compute units need a constant supply of model weights and intermediate data. If memory can't keep up, the expensive chip with tens of billions of transistors literally idles, waiting for the next batch of data. Samsung plans to solve this with HBM5, aiming to double performance relative to HBM4E and increase power efficiency by 20%. The bandwidth of a single stack could approach 4 TB/s with a 4096-bit bus. Let's dive into the details.
